Since the 18th century, tea merchants have employed tasters to evaluate incoming shipments, assess quality, determine fair pricing, and create consistent blends. These professional tasters, historically working in London's Mincing Lane (the center of the global tea trade until the mid-20th century), developed standardized evaluation protocols that remain largely unchanged today. The traditional cupping setup uses white porcelain cups with serrated lids (to strain liquor from leaves), evaluating dry leaf appearance, wet leaf aroma, liquor color, and most importantly, flavor and mouthfeel. A standard cupping brews 2.86 grams of tea in 150ml of freshly boiled water for exactly 5-6 minutes—deliberately over-brewing to reveal both qualities and defects that gentler brewing might conceal. Professional tasters slurp tea from a spoon with a sharp intake of breath, aerating the liquid across the palate to engage all taste and aroma receptors simultaneously. Modern tea sommelier certification programs have formalized this knowledge into structured curricula. The International Tea Masters Association, founded in Belgium, offers a rigorous certification program covering tea botany, chemistry, processing, evaluation, pairing, and service. The Specialty Tea Institute, associated with the Tea Association of the USA, provides progressive certification levels from Tea Sommelier to Tea Master. The UK Tea Academy in London offers diplomas in tea tasting and evaluation. The Global Tea Initiative at UC Davis takes an academic approach, combining sensory science with agricultural research. China's national tea evaluation system, administered through the tea research institutes, maintains the most comprehensive grading frameworks, with specific standards for each tea category and origin. Becoming a professional tea taster requires developing exceptional sensory acuity and an extensive flavor memory. Tasters must distinguish hundreds of flavor notes, identify processing defects, assess quality grades, and communicate their evaluations precisely. The flavor wheel developed for tea—similar to those used in wine and coffee—categorizes descriptors into families: vegetal (grassy, spinach, seaweed), floral (jasmine, orchid, rose), fruity (citrus, stone fruit, berry), nutty (almond, chestnut, hazelnut), spicy (pepper, cinnamon, clove), mineral (wet stone, metallic, chalky), roasted (toasted, smoky, charcoal), sweet (honey, caramel, vanilla), earthy (mushroom, forest floor, leather), and marine (oceanic, kelp, briny). Physical conditioning is part of the profession: tasters typically avoid strongly flavored foods, alcohol, and smoking, as these impair palate sensitivity. Many professional tasters maintain strict dietary discipline on tasting days, beginning with a neutral breakfast and avoiding coffee, spicy foods, and heavy meals. The time of day matters—most tasters find their palate sharpest in late morning, after any overnight palate dulling has cleared but before palate fatigue sets in. Professional tasters may evaluate 200-400 teas in a single session during buying seasons, requiring extraordinary concentration and stamina. Tea and food pairing represents a growing area of sommelier expertise. Like wine pairing, tea pairing considers complementary and contrasting flavor interactions, but tea adds unique dimensions: tannin levels that cut through richness, umami that enhances savory dishes, and astringency that cleanses the palate. General pairing principles include matching intensity (delicate teas with light foods, robust teas with rich dishes), complementing flavors (jasmine tea with floral desserts), and creating contrast (smoky lapsang souchong with sweet foods). Specific pairings that sommeliers frequently recommend include: first flush Darjeeling with fresh goat cheese or light salads; gyokuro with sashimi or delicate seafood; Assam with rich chocolate cake or hearty breakfast foods; aged pu-erh with braised meats or strong cheeses; high-mountain oolong with stone fruits or light pastries; and silver needle white tea with subtle, creamy desserts. Some high-end restaurants now offer tea pairing menus alongside or instead of wine pairings, with tea sommeliers guiding diners through carefully curated selections that evolve across courses. The economics of tea expertise are evolving. Tea sommeliers work in diverse settings: luxury hotels, specialty tea shops, tea import companies, restaurants, spas, and as independent consultants. Some specialize in tea education, conducting workshops and corporate events. Others focus on buying and sourcing, traveling to origins to select teas for companies. The growing specialty tea market supports these careers, as consumers increasingly seek expert guidance in navigating an overwhelming variety of teas. Tea competitions have become important venues for professional recognition. The Global Tea Championship, organized by the World Tea Expo, evaluates teas across numerous categories. The North American Tea Championship provides blind evaluation by panels of certified tasters. China's provincial and national tea competitions set quality benchmarks that directly influence market prices, with award-winning teas commanding premiums of 200-500% over comparable non-awarded teas. These competitions provide professional validation for producers and reference points for industry quality standards.
